title: The Wizard and the Simple Errand
markdown:
Gadzooks, but the Whispering Peaks of Eldoria made a simple errand look like a coronation. Cedar cloaked the slopes. Slate roofs gleamed. Ravens wheeled as if they had been hired for atmosphere. Wizard Alban, a man of measured movements and a sparkling intellect, had a jackdaw named Riddle on his shoulder and a shopping list of one item: a sprig of Moonpetal Bloom from the village market. Calming herb. Straightforward. Over the years, unfortunately, the errand had become a local spectacle.

The square was already busy when Professor Alistair Thorne and Dame Seraphina Meadowlight intercepted him. Vanity travelled with them like a third cloak. Thorne’s robes shimmered with enchantments. He adjusted his spectacles.

“Ah, Alban, our most punctual practitioner! We are here to ensure your errand is imbued with the proper gravitas.”

Seraphina’s silver hair was woven with starlight. “It would be a shame for such a vital herb to be procured without ceremonial blessings and an interpretive dance of the elements. We shall commence the Ritual of Verdant Procurement at once.”

Riddle offered a knowing caw. Alban swallowed a sigh. Destiny, it seemed, had embroidered his shopping list.

Thorne unfurled a shimmering scroll. “Your journey begins with the Azure Arc of Assurance. Observe!” A luminous blue arc appeared over Alban’s head. Villagers murmured, which Thorne took as a standing ovation.

Seraphina countered. “Commendable, Alistair, but it lacks zest. I present the Gilded Zephyr of Zealousness!” Golden motes rained on the arc. “A bit more movement.”

“Static? Mine possesses profound stillness. Yours is chaotic glitter.” Thorne added miniature lightning with exquisite precision.

“And yours lacks soul!” Seraphina conjured ethereal swans. “All angles. No poetry!”

Two goblins perched nearby, scribbling scores for originality and spectacle. Alban watched the duel the way one watches a kettle that has forgotten it was meant to boil water.

“A plan requires directness,” he murmured to Riddle. “This is flamboyant irrelevance.”

“It lacks practical application,” Riddle croaked. “Or, as the proverb I have just coined declares: a good plan, to be truly excellent, requires excessive strangeness, flamboyant displays, and at least three musical interludes.”

Alban excused himself, promising to return with the herb. He knew a place of quiet and culinary timing: Grimble the ogre baker, immense, kind-eyed, and never late with a crust.

Warmth met them at the door, a wall of honey and yeast and the particular comfort of an oven that kept appointments. Flour ghosted Grimble’s enormous forearms. A tray of cakes cooled with military punctuality. “Wizard Alban! And Riddle! A moment of peace from the hurly-burly? Fresh honey-cakes. Just out.” He set two plates as if timing were a kindness, which, in a bakery, it was.

“Your reputation precedes you,” Alban said. “Quiet sustenance. And a loaf of hearth-bread for the journey back.”

Distant magic popped from the square. Thorne sculpted clouds. Meadowlight tried to make cobblestones hum. The goblins’ quills sounded like angry insects.

“Exhausting,” Alban said.

Riddle pecked a crumb. “They compete for glory you can see from a hill. As if magic were a tapestry, not a tool.”

Alban nodded. “Purpose is being overlooked. Your remark about strangeness holds a key. Not more strangeness. Its opposite.”

Riddle tilted his head. “The plot thickens, much like Grimble’s fudge sauce.”

They finished the cakes. Grimble wrapped the loaf with a baker’s exactness and a nod that meant the oven had already forgiven the square. Alban tucked the bread away. “We complete the errand. Without stylistic adjudication.”

Back in the square the fever had risen. Thorne scented the air with roses. Meadowlight conjured dancing moonlight sprites. Villagers watched with the weariness of people who had come for onions and stayed for opera.

Alban, guided by Riddle, skirted the edge toward the herb stall. Thorne spotted him. “Alban! Such a pedestrian fashion? The grand finale!”

“You wouldn’t want to miss the scoring!” Seraphina added.

Alban stopped. His voice cut the din without raising itself. “Your displays are magnificent. I have an errand. It requires sincerity, not spectacle.”

Then he performed the revolutionary act. He walked to the herb merchant and asked for Moonpetal Bloom. He paid with a silver coin. He accepted one pale luminous sprig.

Thorne and Meadowlight froze, mouths open. The goblins looked up, confused, quills dripping.

“But the performance!” Thorne spluttered.

“The points! The categories!” Meadowlight wailed.

Riddle hopped onto a low wall. “He procured the herb. With efficiency. And a clear intention. Thus, the errand is complete.”

Applause moved through the villagers like a sensible breeze. Thorne’s swans, deprived of an audience, sat down on a roof and became ordinary weather. Seraphina’s sprites wandered off to look at actual moonlight, which had been available the whole time. The goblins awarded Alban a category that did not exist until that moment, then argued about how to spell it.

Alban tucked the sprig beside Grimble’s loaf and offered the spellcasters a small smile. On the path back into the peaks, Riddle preened as if he had invented shopping.

“Less likely to attract scorekeeping goblins,” the jackdaw said. “A simple task, done well, keeps its own score.”

Alban broke the hearth-bread and shared the heel. The Moonpetal, unblessed by interpretive dance, smelled like itself. Behind them the square began, slowly, to sell onions again.
characters: Alban (measured wizard of Eldoria), Riddle (knowing jackdaw), Grimble (ogre baker with impeccable timing)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
author: StoryGen Community
